newsitem.title: USA: Clinton to have knee surgery, faces long recovery.
newsitem.headline: Clinton to have knee surgery, faces long recovery.

text.p: President Bill Clinton will have surgery on Friday to repair a torn tendon in his right leg after a late-night fall. Doctors said he would make a full recovery but face weeks of rehabilitation.
The president stumbled on some "irregular shaped" steps about 1:20 A.M. EST (0620 GMT) on the estate of Australian golfer Greg Norman.
He was due to be flown to Bethesda Naval Hospital close to Washington about 9 A.M. (1400 GMT) on Friday morning and was expected to undergo surgery later in the day, the White House said.

Clinton has a torn quadriceps tendon, which connects the kneecap to the upper thigh. Doctors at St Mary's Hospital in West Palm Beach where Clinton was taken for X-rays said he would be expected to make a full recovery.
Dr. Joel Cohen, an orthopedic surgeon at the hospital, told an early-morning press briefing that Clinton's leg would be immobilized in a brace and that he would be on crutches for several weeks.

White House spokeswoman Mary Ellen Glynn said it was too early to say whether Clinton's injury would affect the March 19-20 Helsinki summit with Russian President Boris Yeltsin at which they are due to discuss NATO'S plans to expand eastwards.
Asked whether Clinton would go ahead with the summit, she said: "There are no plans at this time to change his agenda."
The White House said Clinton would be conscious under local anaesthetic during surgery, avoiding a temporary transfer of power to Vice President Al Gore.
"He won't go under (a general anaesthetic)," Glynn said in West Palm Beach. "He'll be alert the whole time."
He is expected to undergo surgery with an epidural block to anaesthetise his right leg.
Doctors said the injury was not uncommon and they described it as minor.

"He has a tear in the quadriceps tendon," Cohen said at a press briefing. "It's not an uncommon injury. The expectation would be a return to full activity. They're going to sew the tendon back to his kneecap. He literally pulled the tendon from the bone," he said. "It was a deceleration injury."

Clinton's personal physician, U.S. Navy Captain Connie Mariano, said the president was in great pain after the fall, but had been given a non-narcotic anti-inflammatory painkiller and remained in good spirits.
"He remembers his right leg buckling out. He has a tear of the quadriceps tendon," Mariano said.
Clinton had asked for a set of playing cards in the hospital and was playing hearts, his favourite game, with White House aide Bruce Lindsay.

Cohen said normally this kind of injury put the patient in a splint and on crutches for several weeks followed by a course of rehabilitation. He said full recovery could take between six weeks and three months.
Glynn said Clinton stumbled on some steps while walking to his guest cottage on Norman's estate after staying up late chatting with the golfer following a political fund-raising dinner in the state.
Clinton was in Florida to play in a two-day golf tournament hosted by Norman beginning on Friday.
He was taken by ambulance to St. Mary's Hospital in West Palm Beach, arriving on a stretcher around 1:45 A.M..
The leg was X-rayed and underwent magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) where the tendon tear was discovered, Glynn said.
